# Residual power concavity of rate defects and legitimate ordinary convex lifts

This note concerns actual GEOMETRIC-CELL inverse-volume rate defects. It
does not identify them with normal surface conditional laws. Their shared
tool is the unequal-radius ball argument. It proves an exact positive-power
density and ordinary convex lift for each nonzero cell/rate component.
A different lift applies to the archived pointed-cone escort limits.
Mixtures, source marks, and cross-fiber compatibility remain explicit.

## 1. Positive measure concavity gives the residual density exponent

Let mu be a nonzero finite compactly supported measure in a Euclidean
space. Suppose for a finite real p>0, compact sets A,B of positive measure,
and 0<t<1,

    mu((1-t)A+tB)^(1/p)
      >=(1-t)mu(A)^(1/p)+t mu(B)^(1/p).                    (1)

Its support S is convex. Put q=dim aff(S). If q=0, mu is one positive
atom. If q>0, then q<=p and:

* mu is absolutely continuous with respect to Euclidean H_q in aff(S);
* mu gives the relative boundary of S zero mass;
* on O=relint S it has a finite positive continuous density g;
* for q<p, the function g^(1/(p-q)) is concave on O;
* for q=p, g is constant on O.

Here is a full proof, including boundary exclusion. Inner regularity
extends (1) to open input balls: compact subsets approach the two masses,
and their Minkowski interpolation lies in the corresponding interpolated
open ball. Positive masses near any two support points thus give positive
mass near each strict convex combination, proving that S is convex.
Identify its affine hull isometrically with R^q. Its interior O is nonempty.

For epsilon>0 set

    f_epsilon(x)=mu(B_epsilon(x))/(omega_q epsilon^q),
    h_epsilon(x)=f_epsilon(x)^(1/p),      x in O.            (2)

All values are finite and positive. Interpolating equal-radius balls in
(1) proves concavity of h_epsilon for every interpolation weight. A finite
concave function on an open convex set is continuous, by the elementary
secant-slope bounds on an interior ball. In particular this continuity
argument does NOT assume sphere-nullness or absolute continuity of mu.
Fubini in the affine hull gives

    integral f_epsilon dx=mu(S).                           (3)

If B_(2r)(x) lies in O, concavity and nonnegativity show that
h_epsilon(y)>=h_epsilon(x)/2 for all y in B_r(x). Hence

    omega_q r^q [h_epsilon(x)/2]^p <= mu(S).                 (4)

Choose r uniformly on a compact subset of O to get uniform local bounds.
On a slightly smaller compact subset these also give uniform Lipschitz
bounds: extend each relevant line a fixed distance in both directions
inside the larger neighborhood, and compare shorter secants with those
longer secants. Arzela--Ascoli and a compact exhaustion therefore give
locally uniform subsequential limits h, finite, nonnegative and concave.

The measures f_epsilon dx converge weakly to mu: the averages of every
continuous compactly supported test over shrinking balls converge
uniformly to the test. Thus any locally uniform limit gives

    mu restricted to O = h^p H_q.                          (5)

Every open ball in O has positive measure by the definition of support.
A nonnegative concave function vanishing at an interior point vanishes
identically: express that point as a strict convex combination of any
other point and a nearby point in the opposite direction. Consequently
h is positive throughout O. Any two continuous subsequential limits
agree almost everywhere by (5), hence everywhere. The local uniform
limit is unique; write g=h^p.

We must still exclude boundary mass. If A=partial_rel S had positive
mass, choose a compact relative ball B inside O with positive mass.
For 0<t<1 the compact set A_t=(1-t)A+tB is inside O, because a relative
ball of radius proportional to t remains inside S around each of its
points. Every point of A_t is within t diam(S) of the relative boundary.
Yet (1) gives

    mu(A_t)>=(1-t)^p mu(A).

The finite measures of the shrinking INTERIOR collars
{x in O:dist(x,partial_rel S)<=epsilon} tend to zero. This contradicts
the positive lower bound as t decreases to zero. Thus the boundary has
zero mass and (5) describes all of mu.

Every point of O is now a differentiation point. Apply (1) to balls
of radii epsilon a and epsilon b centered at arbitrary x,y in O.
Divide by omega_q epsilon^q and let epsilon tend to zero:

    g((x+y)/2) ((a+b)/2)^q
      >=[(g(x)^(1/p)a^(q/p)+g(y)^(1/p)b^(q/p))/2]^p.        (6)

Taking x=y, normalizing a+b=2 and letting b decrease to zero gives
g(x)>=2^(q-p)g(x), hence q<=p. If q<p, maximizing the right side of
(6) uses a:b=g(x)^(1/(p-q)):g(y)^(1/(p-q)) and proves

    g((x+y)/2)
      >=[(g(x)^(1/(p-q))+g(y)^(1/(p-q)))/2]^(p-q).          (7)

Continuity gives full concavity of this power. If q=p, (6) instead
gives g((x+y)/2)>=max(g(x),g(y)). Reflecting sufficiently close interior
points about one another proves equality of their values; connectedness
then gives a constant density. All asserted affine dimensions are covered.

## 2. An exact ordinary convex lift for integral residual exponent

Suppose p is a positive integer and 0<q<p. Put r=p-q and f=g^(1/r).
This positive concave function is bounded on all of O. Fix an interior
point x0 and a small interior ball about it. Express x0 as a convex
combination of any y in O and a point of that ball on the opposite ray.
The weight on y is bounded uniformly below in terms of that ball and
diam(S); nonnegative concavity bounds f(y) by a constant times f(x0).

The upper-limit extension fbar to S is finite, upper semicontinuous,
nonnegative and concave. For the last assertion, approximate two boundary
points by interior sequences attaining the upper limits and pass the
concavity inequality to the limit. Define

    B_mu={(x,u) in S x R^r:
               |u|<=fbar(x)/omega_r^(1/r)}.               (8)

This is a compact convex body of dimension q+r=p. Its allowed radius is
concave, and is positive near every interior x. Uniform p-dimensional
volume projects EXACTLY to mu, because its u-fiber volume is fbar(x)^r=g(x)
almost everywhere, and mu has no boundary mass. Symmetry in u makes its
centroid (bar(mu),0).

Ordinary Grünbaum in dimension p now proves, for EVERY closed affine
halfspace H containing bar(mu),

    mu(H)>=Gamma_p mu(S),   Gamma_p=(p/(p+1))^p.           (9)

This uses the explicit uniform convex body (8), not a false claim that
mu is uniform. When q=p the density is constant and ordinary Grünbaum
applies directly to S. When q=0 every halfspace containing the atom
has its full mass, with the stronger constant one.

## 3. Actual positive-rate geometric-cell inverse defects

The source
candidate 1ec792c66c5ddc47
proves that each actual geometric cell's positive-rate inverse law
gamma_i(t) satisfies (1) with p=d-1. It comes from uniform convex AFFINE
SLICES and their weak limits, not from a surface normal disintegration.
Its finite-cell extension permits delayed thresholds, and the actual
group kernel excludes threshold atoms at positive rates.

The canonical right-continuous versions retain (1) at every positive
post-threshold rate, not merely almost every rate. Approach a rate from
above through convergence rates. The decreasing measures have finite
weak right limits by the local group-kernel bounds; positive measure
concavity is weakly closed by the proof in that source. At a positive
start threshold use its finite right limit. Below it the component is
zero. The finite left limits obey the same conclusion.

In the setting of
candidate 1d07780671b93642,
each nonzero component in one sampled fiber is supported on a zero
face of dimension at most d-2. For q_i(t), the affine dimension of THAT
COMPONENT'S support, Sections 1--2 prove

    0<=q_i(t)<=d-2,
    gamma_i(t)=g_i,t H_(q_i(t)),
    g_i,t^(1/(d-1-q_i(t))) concave on its support interior. (10)

Every non-atomic component therefore has a genuine (d-1)-dimensional
uniform convex lift. Its OWN centroid has the cap guarantee Gamma_(d-1),
strictly larger than Gamma_d. An atom has depth one. Every ambient
physical halfspace restricts to an affine halfspace on this fixed-fiber
support. If its functional is constant there and it contains the
centroid, it contains the full component. Thus no orientations are lost
in this COMPONENTWISE statement.

This centroid need not be an existing source mark, deepest point, or
critical cap contact. It lies on the limiting zero face, generally on
the boundary of a positive d-dimensional original fiber. No depth claim
for the ORIGINAL mixed volume follows.

## 4. Face restriction is all-or-nothing for each component

Let S_i be the convex support of one component in (10), and let A>=0
be affine on the canonical body. If gamma_i(t){A=0}>0, then
S_i is entirely contained in {A=0}. Otherwise A is either a positive
constant on its affine support, giving empty restriction, or its zero
set is an H_q-null proper hyperplane. The atomic case is immediate.
Restriction to a base face likewise retains or discards an entire
fixed-fiber component.

Thus exposed physical-face restriction does not make arbitrary density
cuts inside one geometric rate component. It does NOT make overlapping
face pieces a partition or split the directional cap-payment inequality
into separate cell-label inequalities. Those are known for the actual
aggregate physical defect and its full cap law.

At each positive rate, the aggregate remains a FINITE positive mixture
of components (10), with the precise coefficients from the geometric
group kernel and finite sampled fibers. Their number is not controlled
by the desired parity constant. Arbitrary source allocations can cut
the components further and need not preserve (10). The companion
candidate 6090c7ee45c2de64
gives an actual single-gradient-group mixture with disconnected support
and arbitrarily small depth at its aggregate centroid. It cannot be
substituted into (9).

## 5. Pointed-cone escort limits are a different liftable class

The archived sources
candidate 1389446c1fac70ac
and candidate e70b63e0e6efe01c
prove, under their facet or CLOSED POINTED projected-cone hypotheses,
the tangential escort limit on an m-dimensional face F:

    d sigma(x)=1_F(x)L(x)^(-m-2)dx/E_F(x0),
    L(x)=1+a dot(x-x0)>0,                                (11)

where a is the actual projective-energy minimizer. This is generally
not positively power-concave in the original coordinates: its log
density is strictly convex wherever L varies. It is NOT (10).

It nevertheless has a different exact ordinary convex lift. Center
coordinates at x0 and put

    T(x)=x/L(x),   y=T(x),   ell(y)=1-a dot y=1/L(x).

Positive denominators make T a bijection onto a compact convex body D.
Convexity follows by reweighting convex combinations with the endpoint
denominators. The rank-one determinant formula gives Jacobian
L^(-m-1). The actual minimizing parameter has the first-order condition

    integral_(F-x0) x L^(-m-2) dx=0.

Consequently D has volume E_F(x0) and ordinary centroid zero. Multiplying
L=1+a dot x into the escort integrand also proves
integral L^(-m-2)=integral L^(-m-1)=E_F(x0).

The pushforward of (11) is the AFFINE density

    d(T_*sigma)(y)=ell(y)1_D(y)dy/E_F(x0).                 (12)

Define the compact convex body in dimension m+1

    B={(y,s): y in D, 0<=s<=ell(y)}.                      (13)

Its positive affine height gives nonempty interior. Its volume is
E_F(x0), since the centroid of D is zero. Uniform volume on B projects
to (12). Let bar y be the y-coordinate of B's centroid. Ordinary
Grünbaum yields a Gamma_(m+1) bound for every closed halfspace in the
y coordinates containing bar y. Pull it back to the single point

    x_star=x0+bar y/(1-a dot bar y) in F.                  (14)

All closed halfspaces transfer under this positive projective chart:
after centering, u dot x>=b is equivalent to (u+b a) dot y>=b.
A constant transformed functional gives the full set whenever the
halfspace contains the selected point. Thus (14) has depth at least
Gamma_(m+1) for sigma in every ambient orientation. For m=0 the escort
is an atom and has depth one directly. At codimension at least two
in the original d-dimensional fiber, m+1<=d-1, so this is a genuine
ordinary dimension reduction.

The selected point is generally NOT x0. For F=[0,1] and mark t in (0,1),
the actual parameter and energy are

    a=(1-2t)/(2t(1-t)),   E_F(t)=4t(1-t).

Direct integration gives

    sigma([t,1])=1/4+t/2,
    sigma([0,t])=3/4-t/2.

Although its centroid is t, its depth there tends to 1/4 as t decreases
to zero. It does not inherit the Gamma_2=4/9 CENTROID bound. The
existential point (14) remains valid.

## 6. Scope

The two lifts concern different actual measures: geometric cell/rate
defects have (10), whereas the proved pointed-cone limit gives (11).
Neither identifies these laws, changes the integer lattice, transfers
an existing source mark, or glues their mixtures into one compatible
mixed-integer convex body. Any OC application must retain the actual
aggregate cap constraints and prove the required cap capture of a
legitimate componentwise center.
